title: Model Selection — GPR, Random Forest, and Linear
description: A 2-input dataset with a compact Gaussian-shaped peak centered in the design space, plus a background linear trend — typical of a physical optimum (peak efficiency, resonance, optimal mixture ratio) surrounded by a monotone background. You will train a Linear model, Random Forest, and GPR on the same data and compare results. The exercise shows why model family is the first choice to make and when GPR's smooth interpolation outperforms RF's piecewise approximation.

steps.instruction: The dataset has 2 inputs (x1, x2) in [0, 3] and 1 output (y). The underlying response is a smooth Gaussian-shaped hill centered at (1.5, 1.5) with a linear background trend — it peaks in the middle of the design space and falls off in all directions. A linear model can only fit the background trend; it cannot represent the peak shape at all.

quiz.question: The response has a smooth compact peak centered in the design space, plus a linear background trend y ≈ x1 + 0.5·x2. What will a linear (Ridge) regression model predict for points near the center (1.5, 1.5)?
options: It will correctly predict the peak because Ridge regression can capture any pattern given enough regularization
It will severely underpredict the peak — the model can only fit the linear trend and will predict values close to x1 + 0.5·x2, missing all of the Gaussian contribution
It will overpredict the peak because Ridge amplifies large values
Linear regression always fails when inputs are normalized
quiz.explanation: Ridge regression fits a weighted sum of inputs: ŷ = w0 + w1·x1 + w2·x2. No matter how the weights are chosen, this cannot represent a peaked surface — it produces a tilted plane. All points near the Gaussian peak will have large positive residuals (true value >> predicted). This is not a parameter-tuning problem; it is a model-family mismatch: you need a nonlinear model.

steps.instruction: Open Step 4 — Clean. This synthetic dataset has no missing values or outliers. Skip it and move on.
Designate x1 and x2 as inputs and y as the output.
Apply Min-Max normalization to x1 and x2.
Open Step 8 — Filter Inputs. With only 2 inputs there is no multicollinearity to screen. Skip it and move on.

First run — Linear model: Open Step 9 — Model, select Linear, test split 0.2, 5-fold CV. Train. The R² badge will be red (R² < 0.70). Open the residual plot — you should see large positive residuals clustered in the center of the predicted range, where the model consistently undershoots the Gaussian peak.

quiz.question: The linear model achieves R² ≈ 0.60 (red badge). The residual plot shows large positive residuals at intermediate predicted values and near-zero residuals at low predicted values. What does this spatial pattern in the residuals reveal?
options: The model overfit the training data and the test split was too small

The model is systematically underpredicting the peak region — positive residuals in the middle of the predicted range are the signature of a missed local maximum that the linear model cannot represent
Normalization caused the residuals to cluster
Ridge regularization is set too high
quiz.explanation: When residuals show a spatial pattern (clustering at certain predicted values rather than random scatter), the model is missing a structural feature. Here, the linear model predicts a smooth plane — it gets low and high predictions right for points far from the peak, but systematically predicts too low for peak-region points because it has no mechanism to represent the local Gaussian bump. The residual map is essentially tracing the shape of what the model failed to learn.

steps.instruction: Second run — Random Forest: switch model type to RF, same test split and CV folds. Train. The R² badge will jump to green (R² ≈ 0.97). RF achieves this without any assumption about the response shape — it splits the input space into rectangular regions and averages training values within each region.

quiz.question: Random Forest achieves R² ≈ 0.97 with no assumptions about the response shape, while linear regression achieves 0.60 on the same data. What is the mechanism that lets RF capture the Gaussian peak when linear regression cannot?
options: RF uses more parameters than linear regression, which always improves accuracy

RF partitions the input space into small rectangles through decision tree splits and predicts the average training value in each region — the ensemble of many trees approximates any continuous function without requiring a specific functional form
RF automatically detects and fits Gaussian shapes in the data
RF normalizes the inputs differently, which removes the nonlinearity
quiz.explanation: Each decision tree in the forest splits the input space at specific thresholds (e.g., x1 < 1.2 and x2 < 1.8). The leaf node covering the peak region contains mostly high-value training points, so the prediction there is high. The ensemble average of 100 trees produces a piecewise-constant approximation of the smooth surface. Given enough trees and training data, RF can approximate any continuous function — but the predictions are staircase-shaped, not smooth.

steps.instruction: Third run — GPR: switch model type to GPR, RBF kernel (default), alpha 0.1, same test split and CV folds. Train. R² should be ≈ 0.99 — slightly higher than RF. The improvement is real but small: GPR's smooth interpolation matches the smooth Gaussian-shaped response more naturally than RF's piecewise rectangles.

quiz.question: GPR (R² ≈ 0.99) outperforms RF (R² ≈ 0.97) on this smooth peaked response. What property of GPR explains the edge?
options: GPR uses more training iterations than RF

GPR's RBF kernel assumes the response varies smoothly between training points — exactly matching a Gaussian-shaped surface. RF approximates the same surface with piecewise-constant rectangles, introducing staircase artifacts at boundaries between regions
GPR always outperforms RF when the dataset is small
RF cannot fit responses that have a peak
quiz.explanation: The RBF (Squared Exponential) kernel encodes the prior belief that nearby input points should have similar outputs and that the surface is infinitely smooth. A Gaussian-shaped peak satisfies this assumption perfectly. RF's rectangular partitioning introduces discontinuities at every split boundary — each tree boundary creates a step in the predicted surface. With 100 trees, these steps average out to a decent approximation, but GPR's smooth interpolation requires no such averaging.

steps.instruction: Review all three results in the model history. The ranking is GPR (≈0.99) > RF (≈0.97) > Linear (≈0.60). Both GPR and RF have green badges; Linear has a red badge. The GPR–RF gap is small (~0.02) but GPR also provides prediction uncertainty (σ²) at every new input — RF provides only a point estimate.

quiz.question: GPR is slightly more accurate than RF and provides uncertainty estimates. Why would an engineer still choose RF over GPR in practice?
options: RF is always more accurate on engineering data

GPR training scales as O(n³) in the number of training points — it becomes impractically slow above roughly 5,000–10,000 rows. RF trains in O(n log n) and handles large datasets, mixed feature types, and non-normalized inputs without issue. When the dataset is large or speed matters and uncertainty estimates are not required, RF is the practical choice
RF provides better uncertainty estimates than GPR
GPR requires more hyperparameter tuning than RF
quiz.explanation: GPR's cubic training cost (O(n³)) is the primary practical limitation. For 150 training points it is fast; for 15,000 it would take hours on a single core. RF also naturally handles datasets where some inputs are categorical or untransformed. The choice framework: start with GPR for small, smooth, low-dimensional response surfaces where uncertainty estimates matter; use RF when the dataset is large, mixed-type, or when you need fast retraining. Both beat linear regression whenever the response is nonlinear.

steps.instruction: Final observation: kernel choice matters more than the model label. If you retrain GPR with the Matérn 2.5 kernel and the same alpha, you will get R² indistinguishable from the RBF-kernel result on this smooth surface — the kernels encode smoothness assumptions, not different model families. The hierarchy is: model family first (GP, RF, linear), then kernel choice within the GP family, then hyperparameter tuning.

quiz.question: You have a new dataset with 500 rows, 8 inputs, and 1 output. The response is believed to be smooth but you do not know if it is linear. What is the correct order of model-selection decisions?
options: Choose the kernel first (RBF vs Matérn vs RQ), then model family, then tune alpha and restarts

First decide the model family: try linear (fastest, check if R² is acceptable), then RF or GPR if not. If GPR is chosen, then pick a kernel family. Tune hyperparameters (alpha, kernel length scale) last
Always start with GPR — it is the most general model
Run all models simultaneously and pick the one with the highest training R²
quiz.explanation: The decision hierarchy matters for efficiency. Linear regression trains in milliseconds and is a valid baseline — if it achieves acceptable R², it is the right choice (simpler, faster, more interpretable). If not, move to RF or GP. Within the GP family, kernel choice comes before hyperparameter tuning. Evaluating on training R² alone is wrong — always compare on held-out test data or CV scores. With 500 rows and 8 inputs, both RF and GPR are feasible; at 5,000+ rows, GPR's cubic cost becomes a constraint.
